Internal engineering memo: local AI hardware versus better utilisation

Team,

We need to decide whether to buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what we already own. My recommendation is to improve utilisation first, while keeping a narrow, reversible path to additional capacity. Do not approve a broad hardware purchase yet. Fund a focused optimisation effort now, and revisit procurement after we have reliable measurements of demand, latency, and failure behaviour.

The financial case for buying more machines is easy to overstate. New GPUs or accelerators look like a clean answer because they convert an operational problem into a capital line item. But the real cost is not only the sticker price. It includes power, cooling, rack space, network bandwidth, storage, spare parts, monitoring, staff time, and the opportunity cost of delaying other work. If our current fleet is idle for long stretches, buying more hardware would multiply idle capacity. If it is saturated, buying more may help, but only after we understand whether the bottleneck is compute, memory, data movement, scheduling, or model design.

Latency deserves special attention. Many teams equate “more hardware” with “faster responses,” but latency is often governed by queueing, batching, and tail behaviour rather than raw throughput. A model that is fast on average can still be unacceptable if p95 or p99 latency spikes when traffic arrives in bursts. Local deployment can reduce network dependence and improve privacy, but it can also create brittle capacity plans. If a single node fails, a small cluster may degrade sharply. More hardware can improve resilience, yet it can also spread work across more moving parts and make debugging harder.

Reliability is where the decision becomes less obvious. Local systems are attractive because they keep data inside our environment and reduce exposure to external service changes. They are also harder to operate well. We need to know how often nodes fail, how long recovery takes, whether workloads can be rescheduled cleanly, and whether our monitoring can distinguish a slow model from a sick machine. Without that, a purchase may buy capacity we cannot trust.

Opportunity cost is the argument I would most want to hear from the team. Every week spent configuring new hardware is a week not spent improving prompts, distillation, quantization, caching, retrieval, batching, or evaluation. Those improvements may deliver more user value than additional accelerators. They are also more reversible: if a technique does not help, we can roll it back. A large hardware purchase is harder to unwind.

Reversibility should shape the decision. A lease, a cloud burst, a modular expansion, or a small pilot purchase is easier to reverse than a permanent fleet expansion. A new purchase should be justified by a measured shortfall, not by a hopeful forecast. If demand is genuinely growing, we can still buy later, but we should buy with evidence and with a plan for what happens if utilisation remains low.

My proposed path is a 90-day utilisation review. Instrument queue depth, utilisation, latency percentiles, failure rates, and cost per useful inference. Separate interactive workloads from batch workloads. Test batching, caching, model compression, and scheduling changes. Identify which workloads are latency-sensitive and which are throughput-sensitive. Then estimate the capacity gap under realistic traffic, not peak hype.

If the review shows that current hardware is underused, do not buy more. If it shows a persistent, measured shortfall in a specific workload, buy only the capacity needed for that workload, preferably through a reversible arrangement. If the shortfall is broad and durable, then a larger purchase may be justified, but it should be paired with stronger monitoring, redundancy, and a clear exit plan.

I acknowledge uncertainty. Forecasts are noisy, workloads may shift, and local hardware economics can change with power prices, model efficiency, and vendor pricing. I do not want to pretend the right answer is known. But the evidence we have today points toward disciplined utilisation first. Buying more hardware is a legitimate option, not a default. Let us spend the next quarter turning idle capacity into reliable service, then make the purchase decision with data rather than optimism.

Internal engineering memo: buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation first

Decision needed: whether the team should purchase additional local accelerators and storage for inference and fine-tuning, or invest the same budget in making the existing estate faster, fuller, and more reliable. My recommendation is to improve utilisation first, with a narrowly scoped hardware purchase only after a measured ceiling is demonstrated. The current estate is not idle, but it is also not well used: workloads arrive in bursts, batches are small, models are loaded and unloaded too often, and some jobs wait behind others that could have been scheduled differently. That pattern wastes money in a way that is easy to miss because the hardware appears “busy” on average while still delivering poor latency and low useful throughput.

Cost is the obvious starting point. New GPUs, memory, networking, cooling, racks, and maintenance are not one-time line items; they carry depreciation, power, insurance, staffing, and opportunity cost. If we buy capacity before we understand the demand shape, we may pay for headroom that never fills. The alternative is to spend on profiling, scheduling, quantization, caching, batching, model routing, and observability. Those changes are cheaper, faster to reverse, and more likely to reveal whether the real constraint is compute, memory bandwidth, data movement, or human workflow.

Latency matters because users experience the system as a service, not as a utilization percentage. A model that is 70 percent utilized but queues behind large batches can feel worse than a smaller, well-tuned path that returns answers quickly. We should separate interactive inference from offline batch work, set explicit latency budgets, and measure p50 and p95 rather than averages. If p95 is dominated by cold starts, model loading, or network hops, more hardware will not fix it. If p95 is dominated by sustained compute saturation, then capacity becomes a legitimate question.

Reliability is equally important. Local hardware concentrates risk: a failed node, a bad driver, a thermal event, or a storage hiccup can take down a whole class of work. Improving utilisation must not mean packing nodes so tightly that a single failure becomes a service incident. We need headroom for failover, health checks, graceful degradation, and clear ownership of queues. A system that is 95 percent utilized and fragile is worse than one at 70 percent that degrades predictably.

Opportunity cost is the part that is easy to underweight. Every dollar spent on hardware is a dollar not spent on evaluation, data quality, safety review, developer tooling, or customer-facing reliability. The team is small; the marginal value of a new accelerator is lower if the bottleneck is actually poor prompt routing, stale caches, or uneven model selection. Buying hardware can also lock us into a particular architecture before we know which workloads deserve to be local.

Reversibility favors the utilisation-first path. Software changes can be rolled back, A/B tested, and retuned. Hardware purchases are harder to unwind, especially if they require racks, power, or staffing changes. A bounded pilot is reasonable: for example, one or two accelerators for a proven, latency-sensitive workload, with a fixed evaluation window and a kill criterion. If the pilot shows that utilisation is capped by compute rather than scheduling, then the case for more hardware becomes much stronger.

Uncertainty remains. Demand may grow faster than expected; some workloads may be genuinely compute-bound; and local hardware may be preferable to external services for privacy or latency. I do not know yet whether the current estate can reach the required throughput without new purchases. The honest position is that we should not commit to a large purchase today, but we should not rule out targeted capacity either.

Recommended path: instrument the system for two to four weeks, publish utilization, queue depth, latency, failure, and cost-per-request dashboards, then run a controlled batching and routing experiment. If p95 latency and cost per useful request improve materially and the remaining bottleneck is clearly compute, proceed with a limited purchase. Otherwise, reinvest in software and operations. The decision should be made on measured ceilings, not on optimism about hardware.
